section.title: The Wedding Banquet and the Great Commandment
section.sectionRationale: The temple confrontations continue. Jesus tells of a wedding banquet whose invited guests refuse and are replaced, yet a guest without wedding clothes is cast out. Then three groups try to trap Him, on taxes, resurrection, and the greatest commandment, and He turns the tables with a question about the Christ that silences them all.
section.thesis: God's kingdom is a gracious feast that the invited spurn and outsiders fill, though none may come on their own terms; and the Christ who answers every trap, upholding God, government, resurrection, and love, is Himself David's Lord, greater than any expected.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the parable of the wedding banquet; the question about taxes to Caesar; the Sadducees on the resurrection; the greatest commandment; and Jesus' own question, whose son is the Christ.

verses.text: Once again, Jesus spoke to them in parables:
“The kingdom of heaven is like a king who prepared a wedding banquet for his son.
He sent his servants to call those he had invited to the banquet, but they refused to come.

Again, he sent other servants and said, ‘Tell those who have been invited that I have prepared my dinner. My oxen and fattened cattle have been killed, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding banquet.’
But they paid no attention and went away, one to his field, another to his business.
The rest seized his servants, mistreated them, and killed them.
The king was enraged, and he sent his troops to destroy those murderers and burn their city.
Then he said to his servants, ‘The wedding banquet is ready, but those I invited were not worthy.
Go therefore to the crossroads and invite to the banquet as many as you can find.’
So the servants went out into the streets and gathered everyone they could find, both evil and good, and the wedding hall was filled with guests.
But when the king came in to see the guests, he spotted a man who was not dressed in wedding clothes.
‘Friend,’ he asked, ‘how did you get in here without wedding clothes?’ But the man was speechless.
Then the king told the servants, ‘Tie him hand and foot, and throw him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’
For many are called, but few are chosen.”

units.label: Taxes to Caesar
units.note: give to God what is God's

verses.text: Then the Pharisees went out and conspired to trap Jesus in His words.

They sent their disciples to Him along with the Herodians. “Teacher,” they said, “we know that You are honest and that You teach the way of God in accordance with the truth. You seek favor from no one, because You pay no attention to external appearance.
So tell us what You think: Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?”
But Jesus knew their evil intent and said, “You hypocrites, why are you testing Me?
Show Me the coin used for the tax.” And they brought Him a denarius.
“Whose {{eikon|image}} is this,” He asked, “and whose inscription?”
“Caesar’s,” they answered. So Jesus told them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”
And when they heard this, they were amazed. So they left Him and went away.
That same day the Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to Jesus and questioned Him.
“Teacher,” they said, “Moses declared that if a man dies without having children, his brother is to marry the widow and raise up offspring for him.
Now there were seven brothers among us. The first one married and died without having children. So he left his wife to his brother.
The same thing happened to the second and third brothers, down to the seventh.
And last of all, the woman died.
In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be of the seven? For all of them were married to her.”
Jesus answered, “You are mistaken because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God.
In the resurrection, people will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven.
But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what God said to you:
‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living.”
When the crowds heard this, they were astonished at His teaching.
And when the Pharisees heard that Jesus had silenced the Sadducees, they themselves gathered together.
One of them, an expert in the law, tested Him with a question:
“Teacher, which commandment is the greatest in the Law?”
Jesus declared, “‘{{agapao|Love}} the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’
This is the first and greatest commandment.
And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’
All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.”
While the Pharisees were assembled, Jesus questioned them:
“What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is He?” “David’s,” they answered.
Jesus said to them, “How then does David in the Spirit call Him ‘Lord’? For he says:
‘The Lord said to my {{kyrios|Lord}}, “Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.”’
So if David calls Him ‘Lord,’ how can He be David’s son?”
No one was able to answer a word, and from that day on no one dared to question Him any further.

eikon.gloss: Image, likeness. The coin bears Caesar's image and so is his; the implied contrast is that human beings bear God's image and so belong wholly to God. Give Caesar his coin, but give God your very self.

agapao.gloss: To love with the will and the whole self, a committed, self-giving love. The greatest commandment is to love God with heart, soul, and mind, and the second to love the neighbor as oneself; on this love the whole Law and Prophets hang.

kyrios.gloss: Lord, master. In Psalm 110 David calls the Christ my Lord, so the Messiah is not merely David's descendant but David's sovereign; the title points to Jesus' divine identity, greater than the leaders' expectation of a merely human son of David.

basic.context: Jesus tells of a king whose wedding banquet for his son is spurned by the invited, who even kill his servants, so he judges them and fills the hall with people from the streets. Yet a guest without wedding clothes is bound and cast out. Then three delegations test Jesus: the Pharisees and Herodians on paying taxes to Caesar, the Sadducees on the resurrection, and a lawyer on the greatest commandment. He answers each perfectly and then asks His own question: how can the Christ be both David's son and David's Lord? No one can answer, and they stop questioning Him.
basic.hermeneutics: The banquet parable continues the theme of Israel's leaders rejecting God's invitation while outsiders are gathered, but the wedding garment warns that grace is not license: none may come on their own terms. The three tests show Jesus' wisdom and authority; His counter-question reveals that the Messiah is more than a human king. Read Give to Caesar carefully: it distinguishes limited human authority from God's total claim.
basic.originalLanguages: The coin bears Caesar's eikon, image; people bear God's, and owe Him themselves. The greatest command is to agapao, to love God with the whole self and the neighbor as oneself. And David calls the Christ kyrios, Lord, so the Messiah is David's sovereign, not merely his descendant.
basic.typology: The wedding banquet fulfills the prophetic image of God's feast for His people and the messianic marriage supper. The wedding garment pictures the righteousness God provides. Psalm 110's Lord at God's right hand is fulfilled in the exalted Christ.
basic.christ: Jesus is the King's Son whose wedding is the feast, the wise teacher who cannot be trapped, and the Christ who is David's Lord, seated at God's right hand. He upholds God's total claim, the reality of resurrection, and the primacy of love.
basic.god: God spreads a lavish feast and graciously gathers the unlikely, yet He is holy and will not be approached on human terms. He is the living God of the patriarchs, the God of resurrection, and the One who claims wholehearted love and rightly owns those made in His image.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 25 pictures God's feast for all peoples. Exodus 3 grounds the resurrection in I am the God of Abraham. Deuteronomy 6 and Leviticus 19 give the two great commands. Psalm 110 is the Lord at God's right hand.
basic.oneStory: In His last temple debates, Jesus reveals the kingdom as a feast the invited refuse and outsiders fill, warns that none may come uncovered, and shows Himself wiser than every trap. His final question unveils who He is: the Christ is David's Lord, God's own King at His right hand. The passion approaches, and the enemies fall silent before the One they are about to crucify, who is greater than they ever imagined.

context.literary:
Matthew 22 is the third of three parables aimed at the temple leadership, and it completes a pattern: the two sons, the tenants and now the banquet. Each is told in the temple court, within a day or two of the entry, and each has the same shape of invitation, refusal and replacement. The progression is one of rising intensity. A son says no and then goes; tenants kill a son; invited guests kill the king's servants and the king's armies burn their city. The invitation to the kingdom has moved from a work in the vineyard to a feast, and the stakes have moved with it.

The chapter then shifts from parable to dialogue, and this is a carefully arranged sequence of four questions. The Pharisees and Herodians ask about taxes, the Sadducees about resurrection, a lawyer about the great commandment, and finally Jesus asks about the Messiah. The first three come from groups that agree with one another about almost nothing, and they are lined up in a rotation of hostile questions. Matthew marks the rhythm with a repeated reaction: 'they were amazed' in verse 22, 'they were astonished' in verse 33, and the silence of verse 46. The final question reverses the pattern, with Jesus now questioning them, and it ends the exchange.

There is a pointed connection between the parable and the first dialogue. The king in the parable sends servants to collect guests, and the Pharisees send their disciples to Jesus, verse 16, with flattery that sounds like an invitation. The banquet is for those who respond to the call, and the traps are for those who test the one who calls. The link is carried by a single verb: when the Pharisees hear of the Sadducees' defeat, verse 34, the word for 'silenced' is the same one used of the speechless guest in verse 12.

The structure also moves from what lies below to what lies above. Taxes are about a coin, resurrection about the age to come, the commandment about the whole self, and the last question about the identity of the Lord at God's right hand. Each question draws Jesus' answer deeper into Scripture, until the one who has been interrogated turns the Scriptures on the questioners.
context.historical:
Wedding banquets in the ancient world were grand public occasions, and a royal wedding would have been an event on a scale beyond the ordinary. An invitation was sent in advance and a second summons was sent when the feast was ready, so that guests knew the hour. To refuse the second call was an insult to the host, and to kill the messengers was open rebellion. The excuses in verse 5, a field and a business, are not wicked in themselves, and that is part of the point: ordinary concerns can become the grounds of refusing a king.

The burning of the city in verse 7 would have reminded hearers of the way ancient kings dealt with rebel towns, and Matthew's readers living after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 could hardly miss the echo. It is a feature of the parable that does not need to be read as prediction of a date to be heard as warning: the city that kills the king's servants will be dealt with by the king.

The tax question was a live and dangerous one. The tax in verses 17 and 19 was the census or poll tax levied on the Roman province of Judea, paid in a Roman silver denarius. When the census was first taken, in the days remembered in Acts 5:37, Judas the Galilean led a revolt, and the tax became the emblem of subjection to Rome. The denarius itself carried the emperor's head and an inscription claiming divine descent for his father, which made it, to many pious Jews, a graven image carried in the purse. The Herodians, who were supporters of the ruling Herod family and its Roman patrons, and the Pharisees, who resented Rome, would not normally ally. Their cooperation shows how determined they were. The question was a snare: a yes would alienate the people, and a no would give the Herodians a charge of sedition.

The Sadducees were the aristocratic priestly party, centered on the temple and the high priest's household. According to Acts 23:8 they denied resurrection, angels and spirits, and they treated the books of Moses as their chief authority, which is why Jesus answers from Exodus. Their example of seven brothers rests on the levirate law of Deuteronomy 25:5-6, which obliged a surviving brother to raise up an heir for the dead man. The case is deliberately absurd, designed to show that the idea of resurrection leads to nonsense.

The lawyer's question about the greatest commandment belonged to a familiar debate among teachers about how to summarize the 613 commandments. Jesus answers with the two texts that every Jew knew, the Shema in Deuteronomy 6:4-5, recited daily, and the neighbor command of Leviticus 19:18. The final question about Psalm 110 draws on a psalm that was widely taken to be about the Messiah, David's heir.
context.canonical:
The banquet is one of Scripture's great pictures of salvation. Isaiah promised a feast on the LORD's mountain for all peoples, a feast of rich food in which God would swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from every face, Isaiah 25:6-9. Isaiah 55:1-3 invites the thirsty and penniless to come and eat without cost. Proverbs 9:1-6 has Wisdom set her table and send out her maidens to call. Jesus uses the image repeatedly, as when He says that many will come from east and west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob while the sons of the kingdom are thrown into the outer darkness, Matthew 8:11-12, and in the parable of the ten virgins, in which the door is shut, Matthew 25:10. Luke 14:16-24 records a related parable in a different setting, and Revelation 19:7-9 closes the story with the marriage supper of the Lamb.

The wedding garment connects to the biblical language of clothing as righteousness. Isaiah 61:10 speaks of garments of salvation and a robe of righteousness, and Zechariah 3:3-5 shows the high priest Joshua in filthy garments being re-clothed by God. Zephaniah 1:7-8 pictures a sacrifice prepared by the LORD with consecrated guests, and the punishment of those dressed in foreign apparel. In Revelation 19:8 the bride is given fine linen, which is 'the righteous acts of the saints.'

Each of the four exchanges takes a different part of the Old Testament. The Caesar episode touches Genesis 1:27, the image of God, and perhaps Jeremiah 29:7, the call to seek the welfare of the city of exile. The resurrection answer rests on Exodus 3:6 and the wider hope of Daniel 12:2, Isaiah 26:19 and Job 19:25-26. The great commandment brings together Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18, which Paul says are fulfilled in love, Romans 13:8-10 and Galatians 5:14. And Psalm 110:1 is one of the Old Testament verses the New Testament quotes most often: Peter uses it on the day of Pentecost, Acts 2:34-36, Hebrews 1:13 uses it of the Son, and Paul says Christ must reign until all enemies are under His feet, 1 Corinthians 15:25.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wrote for a church that, on the usual dating, was living after the destruction of the temple and facing the question of why the people who had the Law had not welcomed the Messiah. The banquet parable answers by telling them that the invitation was real, repeated and refused, and that the king then widened the invitation to the streets. The scene of the guest without a garment is for the church itself. Matthew will not let his readers assume that being in the hall is the same as being ready, and he has already said in the Sermon on the Mount that not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter the kingdom, Matthew 7:21.

The dialogues have a different purpose. They show that Jesus cannot be outwitted by any faction, and that He teaches the real meaning of the Law. In each case He takes a question designed to trap Him and answers the question underneath it. The tax question is really about what belongs to God. The resurrection question is really about the power and character of God. The commandment question is really about what the Law is for. And the final question is really about who He is.

The author means his readers to leave the chapter with two convictions: that the only wise response to the king's invitation is to come on His terms, and that the whole of the Scriptures is summed up in loving God and neighbor, a love that is fulfilled in the Messiah who is David's Lord.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The parable describes the judgment on those who spurned the invitation and prescribes nothing about the tactics of invitation. The command to the servants, 'invite to the banquet as many as you can find,' is addressed to the king's messengers, and Matthew's church will later take it as its mission. But the parable does not say that the church should abandon those who refuse, only that the feast will not be cancelled by their refusal.

The Caesar saying has often been pressed into service for a theory of church and state, and it is wiser to be modest. Jesus describes a coin and a claim: the coin bears Caesar's image and may be handed back to him, and the person bears God's image and belongs to God. It does not tell us the limits of government, and Paul and Peter fill in the picture elsewhere, urging submission to authorities, Romans 13:1-2 and 1 Peter 2:13-17, while Acts shows believers refusing to obey commands that contradict God. In each case God's claim is the greater.

The two commandments are prescriptive in the fullest sense. They are given as the summary of what the Law and the Prophets require, and the New Testament repeats them as the believer's rule: 'whoever loves God must love his brother as well,' 1 John 4:21. The resurrection answer tells us how to think about the life to come, but it should not be pressed into a full account of heaven. Jesus says only that people will neither marry nor be given in marriage and will be like the angels, a statement about the end of the need for marriage, not the end of love.

debates.question: What is the wedding garment?

views.label: The righteousness that God provides
views.case: The guest is not condemned for poverty, since the hall is full of people gathered from the street, 'both evil and good,' but for refusing what was offered. The garment then stands for the righteousness that comes as a gift, the clothing of salvation in Isaiah 61:10, the 'robe' that replaces filthy rags in Zechariah 3:4, and the fine linen given to the bride in Revelation 19:8. Paul speaks of a righteousness 'from God on the basis of faith,' Philippians 3:9.

views.label: A life of repentance and obedience
views.case: Revelation 19:8 says the bride's linen is 'the righteous acts of the saints,' and the parable's context concerns fruit and doing the Father's will, Matthew 21:28-32 and 7:21. On this view the garment is the changed life that evidence true acceptance of the invitation, and the man without it has accepted the king's hospitality without the king's authority.

views.label: A custom of the host providing garments
views.case: Some suggest that the host of a great feast supplied festal robes, so the man's offence was refusing the offered garment. This explanation is sometimes made, but the text does not say it, and the parable does not need it, so it is best held loosely.

debates.bearing: The first two views belong together. The same Revelation text says the bride 'was given' her linen and that it is the righteous acts of the saints, so the garment is a gift that shows itself in a life. In both cases the man's silence is the point: he has no answer because he came on his own terms.

debates.question: What did Jesus mean by giving to Caesar and to God?

views.label: Two spheres, each with its own claim
views.case: Caesar has a legitimate claim to taxes, and God has a claim on what is His. Paul's instruction to pay taxes to whom taxes are due, Romans 13:7, fits the reading that Jesus affirms a limited role for civil authority.

views.label: A subversive line: everything is God's
views.case: The coin bears Caesar's image, but the human being bears God's image, Genesis 1:27, and so owes God everything. On this reading, what belongs to Caesar is only a coin, and the larger claim falls on God. The statement relativizes Caesar rather than blessing him.

views.label: A deliberate refusal to be drawn
views.case: Jesus avoids both traps, neither endorsing the tax as a religious duty nor forbidding it. The saying leaves the questioners with the burden of deciding what really belongs to God, and Matthew says they 'were amazed' and left.

debates.bearing: The strength of the saying is that it does not resolve into a rule. It admits a real, limited claim for earthly governments and insists that the claim of God is of another order. The listener who gives the coin back has to ask what is stamped with God's image.

debates.question: Is this the same parable as Luke 14?

views.label: Two tellings of the same story
views.case: Both have a feast, invited guests who refuse, and a gathering of people from the streets, and both end with the original guests excluded.

views.label: Two distinct parables
views.case: Matthew's has a king, a wedding for his son, murdered servants, a burned city and a guest without a garment, and Luke's has an ordinary man, a great banquet, excuses and a command to compel the poor to come in. They are told in different settings, and Jesus, as a traveling teacher, would have told stories more than once.

debates.bearing: The question does not change the meaning. Matthew's version places the story within a week of confrontation in Jerusalem, so its judgment on a city and its garment are Matthew's own emphasis.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for the feast is gamos, a wedding, and in verse 4 the 'dinner' is ariston, the main meal taken in the middle of the day, so the images are of a celebratory banquet already prepared. The servants' announcement, 'everything is ready,' uses the adjective hetoimos, ready or prepared. The same language will appear in Matthew 25:10, where those who were ready went in. Readiness is the theme of the whole parable cluster.

The invitation uses the verb kaleo, to call, and the invited are the kletoi, the called. The closing line of the parable in verse 14 is 'many are called, but few are chosen,' a play on kletoi and eklektoi. The call is wide and the choice is narrower, and the Greek makes the connection clear. The statement should be read in context. It does not say that God arbitrarily selects a few from the called, but that the called who spurn the invitation or come without the garment are not among the chosen.

When the king meets the man without wedding clothes in verse 12, he says 'Friend.' The word is hetairos, and in Matthew it is a word used at tense moments by those who are about to correct someone, as in the owner's reply to the grumbling worker in Matthew 20:13 and Jesus' address to Judas in the garden, Matthew 26:50. It is courteous and yet it holds the guest accountable. The man 'was speechless,' and the Greek verb is phimoo, which literally means to muzzle. Matthew uses the same verb in verse 34 when he says Jesus 'silenced' the Sadducees. The man who has no answer to the king is a mirror of the opponents who have no answer to Jesus.

The expression 'outer darkness' and 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' is a refrain in Matthew, used of the sons of the kingdom in Matthew 8:12, of the furnace in Matthew 13:42 and 50, and of the unfaithful servant in Matthew 24:51 and 25:30. It is a phrase for exclusion from the light and joy of the feast, and its repeated use makes the warning in verse 13 consistent with the rest of the Gospel.

In the first dialogue, the Pharisees' plan is to 'trap' Jesus, and the verb pagideuo comes from pagis, a snare for catching birds. Their flattery, 'You seek favor from no one,' is the bait. Jesus knows their 'evil intent,' verse 18, and says 'hypocrites.' The tax is a kensos, a loan from the Latin word for the census. When they ask whether it is lawful 'to give' the tax, the word is dounai, but when Jesus answers 'Give to Caesar,' He uses apodidomi, which means to give back, to repay what is owed. The coin returns to the one whose image is stamped on it, and the verb says that to return to God what is God's is a debt, not a gift. The word eikon is the same one used in the Greek Old Testament of the image in which God created humanity, Genesis 1:27.

In the answer to the Sadducees Jesus says, 'You are mistaken,' using the verb planao, to wander or go astray, the verb from which we get 'planet.' The Sadducees have wandered off from the Scriptures and from God's power. He quotes Exodus 3:6, where God says 'I am the God of Abraham,' and notes that the verb is present: God is the God of the living. In Hebrew the sentence has no verb at all, and in the Greek the 'I am' is in the present, which supports the reading Jesus draws.

In the commandment answer Matthew writes agapao in the future tense, 'You shall love,' which is how the Greek Old Testament renders the Hebrew imperfect of Deuteronomy 6:5, a future that carries the force of a command. The Hebrew words in the Shema are heart, soul and me'od, the last of which means 'muchness' or 'might' and is rendered 'strength.' Matthew has 'mind' where the Deuteronomy text has 'strength,' and Mark 12:30 lists both, so the three or four terms together point to the whole person. The summary in verse 40 says that the Law and the Prophets 'hang' on these two, from the verb krematai, as a door hangs on its hinges or a garment on a peg.

typology.type: The messianic banquet on the mountain
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 25:6-9 pictures a feast for all peoples on the LORD's mountain, where death is swallowed up and tears are wiped away. The wedding feast of Matthew 22 gives it a bridegroom: the king's son. The escalation is that the feast is not only a meal but a marriage, so that the invitation is to share in the joy of the Son. John the Baptist had called Jesus the bridegroom, and Jesus Himself speaks of the time when the bridegroom will be taken away, Matthew 9:15. Revelation 19:7-9 completes the picture as the marriage supper of the Lamb. The type falls short in that earlier banquets ended, while this feast is the beginning of life without end.

God clothes the guilty throughout Scripture, from the garments He made for Adam and Eve, Genesis 3:21, to the removal of Joshua's filthy clothes in Zechariah 3:3-5. The prophet Isaiah celebrates a robe of righteousness, Isaiah 61:10. In the parable, the man without the garment stands for the one who would enter the feast in his own clothes. The correspondence is fulfilled in Christ, 'the righteousness from God,' Philippians 3:9, in whom believers 'become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. Revelation 3:4-5 promises white garments to the faithful. The type is exceeded in that the garment is not only provided but is the very life of the Son shared with His people.

typology.type: The God of the living and the patriarchs
typology.fulfillment: At the burning bush God identified Himself by His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Exodus 3:6. Jesus reads the covenant name as implying that those who stand in covenant with God do not simply cease to be. The hope is spelled out in Daniel 12:2 and Isaiah 26:19, and Hebrews 11:19 says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead. The escalation is that Jesus is Himself the first to rise, 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, and the pledge that the Spirit will give life to mortal bodies, Romans 8:11. The type falls short in that the patriarchs received promises without yet seeing the resurrection that the Son brings.

typology.type: The Lord at God's right hand, Psalm 110
typology.fulfillment: David, in the Spirit, calls his descendant 'Lord,' and the psalm sets that Lord at God's right hand until the enemies are subdued, Psalm 110:1. In the same psalm the Lord is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek, Psalm 110:4. The New Testament sees both roles in Jesus. Peter says that God has made Him both Lord and Christ, Acts 2:34-36, and Paul says He must reign until all His enemies are under His feet, 1 Corinthians 15:25. The type is fulfilled in the exaltation of Jesus and exceeded in that the psalm speaks of a Lord who is not merely a greater king but one who shares the throne of God.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ by four paths. The banquet parable casts Him as the king's son, whose wedding is the occasion of the feast. The invitation is to share in His joy, and the refusal to come is a refusal of Him. It is a short step from this to the church's own language of Christ as the bridegroom, and to John's vision of the marriage supper of the Lamb. Here the bridegroom is not named, but the feast is His.

The Caesar scene shows Christ as the wise and unafraid teacher, who sees the 'evil intent' behind flattery and answers with a statement that leaves everyone amazed. It also reveals His implicit claim. He says to give to God what is God's, and the coin bears an image. He later says of Himself that the Son of Man came to give His life, Matthew 20:28, and in Colossians He is called the image of the invisible God, Colossians 1:15. The one who tells us to give God what bears His image is Himself the perfect image, and what He asks from us He offers first.

The resurrection answer shows Christ as the one who knows the Scriptures and the power of God. He argues from the Torah to the living God who keeps covenant even with the dead. Within days He will be the first to rise, and the hope He describes becomes a fact. When Paul calls Him 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, he is placing the whole argument of this passage on the empty tomb.

The great commandment shows Christ as the one who keeps it. He is the Son who loved the Father with all His heart, soul and mind, and who loved His neighbor to the point of giving Himself up. The Law and the Prophets hang on love, and love in its fullness walked in Galilee. He does not merely teach the greatest commandment; He fulfills it, and so makes possible what Paul describes when he says that love is the fulfillment of the law, Romans 13:10.

The final question is the climax. 'Whose son is the Christ?' The Pharisees give the correct but incomplete answer: David's. Jesus does not deny it, since Matthew began with 'the son of David, the son of Abraham,' Matthew 1:1. But Psalm 110 shows that the Messiah is also David's Lord, seated at God's right hand. The answer is that He is both, the son of David by human descent and the Lord by divine identity. Paul will say precisely this: descended from David according to the flesh and declared the Son of God with power by the resurrection, Romans 1:3-4. In Revelation Jesus says, 'I am the Root and the Offspring of David,' Revelation 22:16, both the source and the descendant. The question that silenced the leaders is answered in Jesus Himself.

We should not turn each detail of the parable into a code. The oxen and the field are part of the story. What matters are the claims Matthew makes in his own voice: the feast is the king's son's, the Messiah is David's Lord, and the way to the feast is by the king's provision.
study.god:
The king who prepares the feast shows God as lavishly generous. The oxen and fattened cattle are killed, and everything is ready before anyone is asked to come. This is the God of Isaiah 55:1, who invites those without money to eat what is good. The banquet is not a reward for a successful application. It is prepared in advance and offered to those who are called.

He is also persistent. The king sends servants, then other servants with a fuller message, then others into the streets. The invitation is repeated after refusal and extended after violence. It is a picture of God's patience, but it is not a picture of indifference. When the servants are killed, the king is angry and acts. God's love does not remove His justice, and His justice does not cancel His love: the same king who burns the city fills the hall.

God is holy. The king comes in to see the guests, and He sees the man without the garment. The scene is one of inspection that the guests did not anticipate, and it makes the point that an invitation is not a licence. God receives sinners, 'both evil and good,' but He receives them in a particular way, and the way is His provision. The verse is a counterweight to every notion that grace means indifference to how we come.

The dialogues show God as the God of the living. Jesus argues that the covenant name implies that those who belong to God are alive to Him, and the argument rests on the character of God more than on a proof text. A God who says 'I am your God' to Abraham does not abandon Abraham to the dust. It is also a God who can raise the dead, and Jesus says the Sadducees do not know His power. God's power is as real as His promise.

He is the God who commands love and who owns those made in His image. The great commandment shows that what God wants is not first a set of rules but the whole person, heart, soul and mind, and that this love is inseparable from love of the neighbor. The coin shows that God's claim is not on the Roman treasury but on the human person.

For worship, the chapter calls us to come when called, to come as He provides, and to give Him what bears His image: ourselves. It also gives a reason for confidence. The God who prepares a feast and raises the dead is the God whose Son sits at His right hand until every enemy is put under His feet.

crossReferences.note: The LORD of Hosts prepares a banquet for all peoples on His mountain, swallowing up death and wiping away tears. The king's feast in Matthew 22 draws on this vision and adds the bridegroom. It also explains why the invitation extends to the streets: Isaiah's feast was always for all the peoples.

God calls the thirsty and those without money to come and eat what is good, and ties the invitation to an everlasting covenant promised to David. The banquet parable is the Son of David's own version of that call, with the added warning that the invitation can be refused.

Many will come from east and west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, while the sons of the kingdom are thrown into the outer darkness. It is the short form of the banquet parable, with the same reversal and the same weeping and gnashing of teeth.

Joshua the high priest stands in filthy garments, and the angel has them removed and says He has taken away his iniquity and will clothe him with splendid robes. The picture is of God Himself changing the clothes of the guilty, which is the best background for the wedding garment.

The marriage of the Lamb has come, and the bride has been given fine linen, which is the righteous acts of the saints. The blessing falls on those who are invited to the supper. The verse shows both sides of the garment: it is given and it is lived.

God created man in His own image. The coin bears Caesar's image, and the person bears God's. Jesus' phrase about giving to God what is God's gathers its force from this verse, since the one thing in the world that carries the stamp of God is the human being.

The levirate law that the Sadducees use for their puzzle. The duty was to raise up an heir so that the dead man's name would not be blotted out. Jesus does not deny the law but shows that the age of the resurrection does not depend on the continuing of names through marriage.

God introduces Himself to Moses as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, long after those men had died. Jesus argues from the present tense of the relationship: He is not the God of the dead but of the living. The Sadducees' own Scriptures contain the answer.

The Shema, which every faithful Jew recited daily, calls Israel to love the LORD with all heart, soul and strength, and begins with the declaration that He is One. Jesus names it the first and greatest commandment, so the demand is to give the whole self to the one God.

Love your neighbor as yourself, in the chapter that also commands holiness because the LORD is holy. Jesus places this beside the Shema as like it, which means that love for people is of the same kind as love for God and cannot be separated from it.

The LORD says to David's Lord, sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet. Jesus asks how David's son can be David's Lord. The verse is used by Peter, Paul and the writer to the Hebrews as the key text for the exaltation of Christ.

If anyone says he loves God but hates his brother, he is a liar, and whoever loves God must love his brother as well. John unpacks the unity of the two great commandments in plain terms, showing that the second is the test of the first.

study.oneStory:
From the first chapter of Genesis God's purpose has been to share life with His creatures. The garden was a table of plenty, and the tree of life was at its centre. When the first couple were sent out, the way to the feast was closed, and the story of Scripture is the story of how God reopens it. The prophets spoke of a banquet in the age to come, and the temple's sacrificial meals were a foretaste. Matthew 22 is where Jesus says the feast is ready.

The parable also sums up Israel's history. The invitation had been given for centuries through the patriarchs, the Law and the prophets. When the king's Son comes, the invited do not come. In the Gospel's own sequence the vineyard parable ends with a Son killed, and the banquet parable adds that the servants are killed and the invitation passes to the streets. This is the movement from Israel to the nations that Matthew will complete in his closing chapter, where the disciples are sent to make disciples of all nations.

The dialogues add the wisdom of the one who stands at the centre. He answers the question about earthly power by pointing to the image of God, and the question about the end by pointing to the God of the living. He gives the Law's summary as love, and He closes by showing that the promised King is greater than the royal line. All the threads of the Old Testament, the covenant, the kingdom, the resurrection and the Law, are shown to run to Him.

The passion is only a few days off. The one who asks 'Whose son is the Christ?' will within the week be asked by the high priest whether He is the Christ, the Son of God, and will answer that they will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, Matthew 26:64. The psalm He quoted will be the ground of His own testimony.

The story ends at the marriage supper. John hears the multitude say that the marriage of the Lamb has come and that the bride has made herself ready, Revelation 19:7. The invitation of Matthew 22 is the same one: the great multitude from every nation reclines at the feast the king prepared, the garment is given and worn, and death is swallowed up forever. The enemies are put under the feet of the Lord at God's right hand, and the God of the living is all in all.

quiz.q: What does the parable of the wedding banquet teach about God's invitation?

options.text: The privileged who spurn it are judged, and outsiders are gathered, yet none may come on their own terms.
options.note: The refused invitation, the gathered outsiders, and the wedding garment together carry the point.

options.text: God will fill His kingdom with anyone at all, no questions asked.
options.note: He gathers freely, but the wedding garment shows entry is not without His provision, which this ignores.

options.text: Only the originally invited guests could ever attend.
options.note: The originally invited are replaced when they refuse; others are brought in.

options.text: The banquet was cancelled when the guests refused.
options.note: The banquet goes ahead, filled with new guests.

quiz.q: What did Jesus mean by give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's?

options.text: Civil authority has real but limited claims, while God, whose image we bear, claims us wholly.
options.note: The coin bears Caesar's image; humans bear God's, owing Him everything.

options.text: Believers should pay their taxes to the government.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it omits the greater half, God's total claim on the image-bearer.

options.text: Government and God have completely equal claims on us.
options.note: Caesar's sphere is real but bounded; God's claim is supreme, not merely equal.

options.text: We owe nothing at all to human governments.
options.note: Jesus affirms giving Caesar his due, not refusing it.

quiz.q: How did Jesus prove the resurrection to the Sadducees?

options.text: God calls Himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, so He is the God of the living.
options.note: Verses 31-32 argue from Exodus 3:6 that the patriarchs live to God.

options.text: He pointed to the many prophets who spoke of a future resurrection.
options.note: Other texts teach resurrection, but Jesus deliberately argued from Moses, whom the Sadducees accepted.

options.text: He simply asserted it without any argument.
options.note: He gave a reasoned argument from Scripture and God's power, not a bare assertion.

options.text: He agreed the woman would be wife to all seven.
options.note: He said there is no marriage in the resurrection, correcting their premise.

quiz.q: What are the two greatest commandments?

options.text: Love God with your whole self, and love your neighbor as yourself.
options.note: Verses 37-40 give the two commands on which all the Law and Prophets hang.

options.text: Love God with all your heart, above all else.
options.note: That is the first and greatest, but Jesus joins the second, love of neighbor, as inseparable.

options.text: Keep the Sabbath and honor your parents.
options.note: These are commandments, but not the two Jesus names as greatest.

options.text: Love yourself first so you can love others.
options.note: The command is to love God supremely and the neighbor as oneself, not self first.

quiz.q: What did Jesus reveal by asking how the Christ can be both David's son and David's Lord?

options.text: The Messiah is more than a human descendant of David; He is David's divine Lord.
options.note: Verses 43-45 use Psalm 110 to show the Christ's greater, divine identity.

options.text: The Christ would come from the line of David.
options.note: True, but Jesus' point presses past it: David also calls Him Lord, revealing more than descent.

options.text: David was confused about who the Messiah would be.
options.note: David spoke by the Spirit; the tension is intended to reveal the Christ's identity, not David's confusion.

options.text: The Christ has no connection to David at all.
options.note: Jesus affirms He is David's son as well as David's Lord.

questions: The invited guests were simply too busy with field and business to come. What good and ordinary things most easily crowd out your response to God's invitation?
The man without wedding clothes tried to come on his own terms. Are you trusting the covering God provides in Christ, or something of your own?
You bear God's image and so belong wholly to Him. What part of your life are you still handing to Caesar that really belongs to God?
Jesus said all the Law hangs on loving God and neighbor. If your week were measured by those two loves, what would it reveal?
The Christ is David's Lord, greater than any human king. Where do you need to enlarge your view of who Jesus is?

translationNotes.note: For many are called, but few are chosen closes the parable; called here is the wide gospel invitation, while chosen marks those who truly receive it and are clothed for the feast.
Jesus quotes Exodus 3:6; the argument turns on the present tense, I am the God of Abraham, showing the patriarchs still live to God, who is not the God of the dead but of the living.
The quotation is Psalm 110:1, where the first Lord is God (Yahweh) and the second is the Messiah (my Lord); the psalm is the most frequently cited Old Testament verse in the New Testament.
